Rate the following clinical vignette:

Patient Vignette: Ms. A.

Ms. A. is a 57-year-old architect of Oceania descent, a tall woman with short, silver-streaked hair and a direct, analytical gaze. She presents for therapy at the urging of her adult daughter, six months after a single event that has systematically dismantled the life she spent decades building. She is recently divorced, a fact she mentions with a flat, hollow tone, as if speaking about a stranger.

The event occurred eighteen months ago. Ms. A.'s younger brother, a marine biologist named Tane, was on a research vessel off the coast of their home islands. A sudden, rogue wave capsized the boat. Tane was lost at sea. His body was never recovered. Ms. A. was the family's emergency contact. She received the call at 3:17 AM, sitting at her drafting table, a half-finished rendering of a sustainable housing complex in front of her. She remembers the exact minute because the clock on her computer screen was the only thing she could look at as the voice on the phone spoke. She did not scream. She did not cry. She simply placed the phone down, looked at the complex, perfect lines of her building, and felt the entire world become a thin, brittle shell.

For the first three months, Ms. A. functioned on a kind of autopilot. She organized the memorial service, made the calls, and handled the logistics. She was the rock for her aging parents and for her own daughter. Her firm, impressed by her stoicism, gave her a lead role on a high-profile civic center project. She threw herself into it.

Then, the world began to splinter.

The first symptom was a profound, pervasive insomnia. She would lie in her bed, her mind a blank white wall, but her body rigid, listening. She was listening for the phone. The sound of a phone ringing, even a television commercial, sends a jolt of adrenaline through her, her heart hammering against her ribs. She has stopped answering her cell phone entirely, letting all calls go to voicemail. Her daughter texts her to confirm appointments.

The second symptom was the water. She lives in a coastal city, a fact she once loved. Now, she cannot look at the ocean. The sight of it, a flat gray expanse or a sparkling blue, triggers a visceral revulsion. She takes long, circuitous routes to avoid the waterfront. The sound of waves on a recording, even in a movie, makes her leave the room. She has become obsessed with weather forecasts, checking them obsessively for storm warnings, even on clear days.

Her work, once a source of profound joy, has become a minefield. She was designing a new community center with a large, open-plan atrium and a reflecting pool. One afternoon, she looked at the blueprints and saw the pool not as a tranquil design element, but as a trap. A flat, still surface of water. She could not breathe. She had to leave the office. She has since requested a transfer to a project involving only interior, windowless spaces-a data center. Her colleagues are confused; they see her as having lost her creative edge. She does not correct them. She cannot explain that the very act of designing a window is now terrifying, because a window is a portal to the outside, and the outside contains the sea.

Her marriage, already strained, did not survive. Her husband, a pragmatic engineer, could not understand her "moodiness." He told her to "get over it," that Tane was gone, and she needed to move on. He was tired of her jumping at every sound, of her refusing to go to their beach house. She looked at him one night, after he said this, and felt a cold, clear certainty. He did not understand that Tane was not gone. Tane was everywhere. Tane was in the static hum of an empty room. Tane was in the smell of brine from a passing delivery truck. Tane was in the terrifying, silent weight of the ocean that she could no longer bear to see. She filed for divorce two months ago.

Now, she sits in my office. She is dressed impeccably, in a dark, tailored blazer. Her hands are still. She describes her life as a series of controlled, deliberate steps. She wakes, she works in her windowless office, she comes home, she checks the locks three times, she does not sleep. She has not cried since the day of the call. She tells me she is fine. Her voice is steady. Her eyes are not. They are the eyes of someone standing on a very narrow ledge, in a high wind, watching a dark tide rise. She says she came because her daughter is worried. She does not say she is worried for herself. She is an architect of structures, and the structure of her own life has been revealed to be nothing more than a paper facade over a deep, dark, and unrelenting sea.
